To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the average effect size of non-native plant invasions on native biodiversity is negative (− 0.25) but the distribution of effect sizes is skewed towards the positive (Kuebbing et al. 2020).

the majority of non-native plant impacts are negative, that the impacts of non-natives are often greater than those of natives, and that non-native plants can have significant negative impacts on biodiversity, even in the absence of other stressors.

1) there is a lack of consensus in the invasion literature on whether non-native species have a negative impact on native biodiversity; 2) the meta-analytical approach used by Kuebbing & Nuñez to assess the impact of non-native species is flawed; and 3) the results of their meta-analysis are not generalizable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the potential for over-generalisation of negative impacts of non-native species.
the risk of generalisation from a biased set (Kuebbing & Núñez 2015) of non-native species to many others.
the potential for bias in the literature, not with the average impacts of non-native species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impacts of non-natives vary widely and are difficult to predict (Guerin and Richardson 2018; Davis and Chew 2018).

the average impact across non-native species on native species is negative (Guerin and Richardson 2013), but that the average impact may not be a good predictor of individual cases, and that the average impact can be expected to be highly variable across systems (Boltovsoky et al. 2008).

non-native species may have significant negative effects, and that these effects can be generalised across species, but that the extent to which they do so is unclear, and that the impacts of many non-native species are unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have no objection to the use of invasion science to manage problematic non-native species, but we caution against the use of invasion ecology to generalise across non-native species.
the impacts of non-natives are highly context-specific and can be either positive or negative, depending on the species, the environment, and the scale of the study.
there is no consensus on whether non-native species have a negative impact on native species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the literature has been biased towards negative impacts, and this bias may be due to selection effects in the research process (Guerin 2018).
the evidence for negative effects of non-native plants on native plants and animals has not been rigorously tested.
the impacts of non-natives are context-dependent, and that generalisations are risky.
